article.title: Iran, Neoliberalism, Nihilism, and the Global Order A Conversation with Wendy Brown
article.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
article.content: Conducted in early 2026, on the eve of the assault on Iran by Israel and the USA, this interview with Wendy Brown explores the transformation of the state under finance capital and the intensification of social nihilism. Although publication was delayed due to the interviewer’s travel to Iran, Brown’s analysis of the “global construction” of the Iranian predicament and the “privatisation of the state” remains strikingly prescient and conceptually vital for understanding the current crisis. From the “equal right to inequality” to the extraction of profit from destruction in Gaza, the conversation offers a rigorous materialist map of the neoliberal ruins we inhabit Mohammad Hadi : Although the timing of this conversation coincides with the tragic situation in Iran and the killing of many innocent people – a disaster that casts a shadow over thought, or at least my own – I began this conversation with some difficulty. I have been grappling with a stifling force that shrinks the space for reflection. A voice from both inside and outside tells me that I should only think of what is happening in Iran. This position not only comes into contact with the logic of identity politics but also displays a harsh criticism: why, at this particular historical juncture, turn one’s attention instead to a discussion of neoliberalism? Wendy Brown : I don’t know if I can help you, but I am going to engage your question. To understand the predicament of Iran, one has to move outside of Iran and think about imperialism. We must look at least as far back as the US positioning itself in relation to the Shah as a puppet power, and a larger Middle East politics that has been negotiated and changed over the course of the Cold War and the post-Cold War period. To think about the extraordinary uprising in Iran of the past month – the tremendous courage and sacrifice so many Iranians made in struggling for an opening and a new arrangement of power – one is already forced to think about the global construction of the Iranian predicament. The Iranian situation is never just about Iran. The place of neoliberalism here is significant. There is nothing the revolution of neoliberalism did not touch; in the past fifty years, nothing on the globe has been unaffected by globalisation, deregulation, privatisation, and the aiding and abetting of corporate and finance capital. Neoliberalism brought a fundamental transformation of the international order, which we have recently seen brought to something of an end in the squaring off between China, Russia, and the US. We see an absolute indifference to the fates and conditions of everyone else and the resurrection of a “spheres of influence” foreign policy by the remaining hegemons. Neoliberalism matters as a way of understanding parts of what has happened to the global order and parts of what has happened in Iran itself: making life unaffordable, the economy tanking, and the currency in a mess. While it doesn’t explain everything, especially the specific timing of the uprising, it has intensified the immiseration of the Iranian people beyond the level of state repression or the enforcement of Islamic law. MH : You have argued that neoliberalism is not just an economic programme, but also a governing rationality that reshapes how we understand freedom, responsibility, and even ourselves as political subjects. How would you explain this broader project to someone encountering your work for the first time? WB : We need to offer recognition where it is due: this is an idea that Michel Foucault helped the world understand. Foucault grasped that neoliberalism was not just a set of economic policies – though it does comprise deregulation, privatisation of public goods, and stripping the welfare state. The important thing is that these policies are part of a larger order of political reason or political rationality. He helped us understand the shift from liberalism to neoliberalism as one involving a transformation of the state, society, and the individual subject. With neoliberalism, the state becomes a more overtly constructivist actor; it is turned to construct and support markets, not just to get out of the way like the “night watchman” state of classical liberalism. It is actively engaged in the facilitation of capitalist accumulation. Unlike the Keynesian or social state, which is redistributive, neoliberals wanted a state that would support capital with the recognition that capital does not run with ease by itself; it needs the support of political policy and legal codes. Furthermore, neoliberal reason involves an assault on the very idea of “the social”. Margaret Thatcher famously declared there is no such thing as society, and F.A. Hayek referred to the social as a “dangerous fiction”. Individual subjects are changed from citizens into bits of “human capital” in every aspect of their lives. We see young people preoccupied with rankings, ratings, and followers, which signifies a preoccupation with their ability to attract investors to themselves. This transformation breaks us up into individual entrepreneurial units that either sink or swim, as opposed to being gathered into a social whole. There were dimensions of this project that the original neoliberal intellectuals had not counted on. They did not anticipate the extreme inequality and precarity that would produce a highly activated, angry population – what we call populism on both the Right and the Left. They also did not count on financialisation – the growth of the finance sector at the expense of every other aspect of the economy. The final coup of neoliberalism was not just to privatise public goods, but to privatise the state itself. The financialisation of the state – the overtaking of the state by private finance – is the subordination of states to capital. The original neoliberals counted on the state being able to manage different aspects of markets to facilitate capital; they didn’t count on states being so overtaken by capital that they become the servants while finance is the master. This rationality gets into our heads; we think constantly about how to enhance our capital value and prevent its depletion. MH : Ideals such as freedom, tolerance, rights, and individual choice appear not only as democratic achievements but also as sites where power operates in subtle ways. How do these values become detached from democratic equality and redirected toward exclusion or authoritarian forms of politics? WB : One way to answer this is to note the extent to which neoliberalism has intensified a nihilism already developing in Western culture. Nihilism, theorised by thinkers like Nietzsche and Weber, suggests that, once science and reason displace the authority of God, you lose the fundamental foundations of values. Reason and science only explain how things work; they do not explain what to value. Neoliberalism puts this nihilistic project “on steroids” by claiming all there is to life is economic action. We are reduced to homo economicus across every aspect of life, from dating and mating to education and choosing friends. On a more specific level, consider the values of equality, liberty, and fraternity. Equality is reduced to the “equal right to win or lose in a market” – the equal right to inequality. Liberty becomes the right to do or say anything that enhances your competitive positioning, including the right to be insulting or egregious. Liberty is reduced to a private property right where you are the property. Fraternity simply doesn’t exist in a neoliberal order. The social contract, which says the government should assure minimal thresholds of survival and solidarity, goes away. Freedom, once understood as participation in popular rule, loses its political dimension. MH : I have been struck by the thought that neoliberalism is a great plunderer, but its theft is not limited to the rights of its own citizens. It operates through a profound deception: while it dispossesses its own citizens of welfare and rights, it presents a veneer of legitimacy elsewhere, promising “freedom” to other lands while actually expropriating the possibility of citizenship and democratic capacity. WB : If I understand your comment correctly, you are suggesting that under the guise of freedom, neoliberalism strips human beings of every other aspect of survival. The US experiment in Iraq is a superb example. After toppling Saddam Hussein, the effort to neoliberalise the country involved denationalising banks and making all of Iraq’s assets available for external investment and plunder. It was all done under the sign of freedom, but it intensified long-simmering conflicts, brought the Taliban to Iraq, and cast many Iraqis into poverty and death. Indebtedness is one of the great tricks of neoliberal austerity; it transforms regions into indebted ones from which they can never climb out, producing a desperate population that may turn to the right, the left, or simply submit. MH : In In the Ruins of Neoliberalism , you wrote that the neoliberal critique of social justice in the name of traditional moral norms has become “common sense”. Figures like Trump, Orbán, or Musk, and even Iranian monarchists, pursue a form of authority that promotes traditional values – family, hierarchy, masculinity – in constant interplay with the fluidity of the market. What does this coexistence between a rigid command and market fluidity mean to you? WB : This is an interesting problem because there has always been a strong tension between the right-wing endorsement of traditional values and the “free market”. Irving Kristol, a founder of neoconservatism, withheld a “third cheer” for capitalism because he understood it had a terrible effect on morality and tradition. Capitalism is an innovative, constantly destructive order. Today’s “postliberals” want to affirm capital while using the state to attenuate its effects. They use the state to support families, transform education toward tradition and away from critical thinking, and allow a post-secular religious order to unfold. You see this in Modi’s India, Orbán’s Hungary, and Iran. Orbán uses heavy statism to support a moral-theological project even as capitalism undoes it. Their task is to manage that contradiction – to use the state to offset capital’s effects and ward off reformers who challenge gender norms or reproductive freedom. Figures like Trump are manifestly immoral and non-religious, yet they speak the political discourse of tradition. This resonates with the Iranian diaspora, who may not be religious but stick to traditional values to ward off the perceived “wreckage” of modern life. MH : Neoliberal rationality systematically outsources political judgment and responsibility to market metrics and technocratic governance. I would suggest further that to preserve its legitimacy, this order also outsources its “negative residuals” – violence, failures, and ethical debts – onto other actors or distant abstractions. Morality itself is removed from the centre of political life and reassigned to distant humanitarian spectacles. WB : I wonder if “disavowal” is a better word. The quintessential example is the original neoliberal experiment in Chile. The tremendous violence – people being shot in stadiums – was disavowed by the “Chicago Boys” for years. Neoliberalism prefers “soft power” and managerial language, yet it engages in “slow violence” – sinking masses into despair or uprooting lives through industrial transformation. Neoliberalism has a language of intense disavowal, calling “hostile takeovers” “private equity” to make the takeover of housing and healthcare sound decent. This disavowal permits scapegoating; when life becomes unaffordable, people point to what is near, blaming immigrants, feminists, or elite politicians for their suffering rather than the takeover of buildings by private equity. MH : When it comes to violence, I still tend toward the word “outsourcing”. I am thinking of Mary Kaldor’s distinction between “old” and “new” wars, where conflicts are defined by fragmented constellations of state, non-state, and private actors. Violence is dispersed and contracted out. In Iran, the scale of war is effectively transferred to the people themselves. Civilians are mobilised through calls and incitements from outside – the US, Israel, or the son of the Shah – to go to the streets, which results in more repression. War is displaced onto intermediaries; populations and bodies carry the cost. WB : That is an interesting point. War is now disseminated throughout political and economic spaces; it is no longer just sovereign nation versus sovereign nation. We see this in trade and tariff wars that intermingle national security with economic advantage. There is a loss of boundedness between these spheres. I would add “terror” to this spectre of war. Protesters struggling against state power in both Iran and the US are declared “terrorists” by the very military enacting terror toward the people. The people are recast as illegal combatants. MH : Neoliberalism also appropriates perspectives that appear emancipatory. Some on the left emphasise horizontalist accounts of politics. Thinkers like Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri posit the end of sovereignty as if the age of governing authority is concluding. I regard their claim primarily as a description of what is happening under neoliberalism rather than a form of resistance. What do you think? WB : I completely agree. Sadly, both anarchism and horizontality, when closely read, are often effects of neoliberal discourse rather than resistances to it. Anarchy is essentially a version of the extreme neoliberal aspiration: no rules, no state, just a natural order emerging from individual actions. The “post-sovereign” fantasy is the original neoliberal fantasy: that capital moves freely while navigating a diminished sovereignty. Hardt and Negri would have to rethink their thesis today. Sovereignty is having a huge symptomatic expression as it goes down, seen in the repression of dissent by individual sovereigns. MH : Finally, neoliberalism can even derive benefit from failure, injustice, and terror. We see “predatory wolves” excited to rebuild the “Riviera of Gaza” out of a nightmare of destruction and genocide. Trump, for instance, refrains from direct war with Iran because he must first discern how to convert the circulating violence and fear into advantage. WB : Watching the “predatory wolves” so excited to begin rebuilding the “Riviera of Gaza” was a perfect expression of this. There was excitement about possible development opportunities coming out of that nightmare of genocide, ecocide, and scholasticide. Neoliberalism is exceptional at taking destruction and extracting the last bit of profitability from it. You see this in asset managers who get excited about driving industries into the ground to extract what they can in their death throes. Your description is poetic and unfortunately accurate. The only note of promise I want to end on is that a great many people in the world have had it with this mode of organisation and planetary destruction. You are seeing signs all over the place – not just a turn to fascism, but a turn to resistance and the building of futures that have a different order of things at their heart.
